section_summary: Pages 114-120 conclude the textbook “Japan—Where Ancient Loyalties Survive,” discussing tensions between tradition and modernization, economic inequality, militarism, political violence, nationalism, and changing gender roles, followed by a bibliography; page 121 contains related correspondence. The remainder is a secret interdepartmental file on suspected Japanese espionage and propaganda in Hawaii, especially intelligence-gathering by visiting naval vessels and the tanker Ondo, assisted by local contacts. It includes military reports, witness letters, proposals for coordinated federal action, and a Navy legal opinion concerning the Espionage Act, Hawaiian territorial law, and the 1911 United States–Japan treaty.

subfiles.title: “Japan—Where Ancient Loyalties Survive”: concluding discussion and references for teachers
subfiles.about: The excerpt analyzes the social and political conflicts produced by Japan’s modernization and concludes with a selected bibliography for teachers.
subfiles.summary: The text contrasts imported parliamentary and industrial institutions with persistent clan authority, paternalism, agricultural poverty, and traditional gender expectations. It discusses military expansion, economic inequality, nationalism, political assassinations, the February 1936 coup attempt, and whether Japanese reactionary movements should be considered fascist. Quotations from Shidzue Ishimoto illustrate the pressures exerted on women and former liberals, and the final page lists English-language references on Japanese history, politics, economics, labor, and international relations.

subfiles.title: Letter acknowledging Hornbeck’s inquiry about “Japan—Where Ancient Loyalties Survive”
subfiles.from: Helen Wiss, secretary to Frederick V. Field
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Helen Wiss acknowledges Hornbeck’s letter concerning the textbook and promises to place it before Frederick V. Field when he returns from California.
subfiles.summary: Wiss says Field is at an Institute conference in California and holds Hornbeck's August 14 letter for his return.

subfiles.title: Memorandum recommending State Department participation in discussions of Japanese activities in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: The Far Eastern Affairs Division recommends that its chief represent the State Department in preliminary interdepartmental discussions about suspicious Japanese conduct in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Memo recommends State participate in discussions on alleged objectionable activities by Japanese visitors and residents in Hawaii, involving State, War and Navy and possibly other departments.

subfiles.title: Letter requesting a State Department representative for preliminary Hawaii security discussions
subfiles.from: U.S. Secretary of War Harry H. Woodring
subfiles.about: The Secretary of War requests a State Department representative for preliminary discussions on preventing Japanese activities considered harmful to national defense in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Woodring forwards secret information on visiting and resident Japanese in Hawaii and proposes interdepartmental measures before the presidential committee meets; General Krueger will represent War.

subfiles.title: Presidential letter establishing an interdepartmental committee
subfiles.about: President Roosevelt establishes an interdepartmental committee to seek a practical solution to the Hawaii security problem.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt calls for cooperation among seven departments, designates the Secretary of War as chairman and directs that the information remain secret.

subfiles.title: Joint War and Navy Departments letter on espionage in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Harry H. Woodring, Secretary of War, and Claude S. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The War and Navy secretaries describe measures and proposed legislation intended to curb suspected Japanese espionage in Hawaii and urge broader government cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Joint War-Navy letter: intelligence keeps suspect lists but complete exclusion of foreigners from strategic Hawaiian islands is impracticable; cites executive orders and proposed bills on alien fishing vessels and photography; urges legislative priority and multi-department participation.

subfiles.title: Report of meeting on Japanese naval and training-vessel activities in Hawaii
subfiles.to: Commanding General, Hawaiian Department, and Commandant, Fourteenth Naval District
subfiles.about: The committee reports evidence suggesting that Japanese naval tankers and training ships used repeated Hawaiian visits for reconnaissance, local contacts, and nationalist propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The report inventories Japanese cruisers, oilers, and merchant training vessels visiting Hawaiian ports and argues that the tankers’ detours lacked a convincing logistical purpose. It recounts photography, sketching, measurement of docks and installations, visits to suspected local contacts, and the timing of voyages to coincide with American exercises and aircraft movements. It emphasizes the vulnerability of the Kona coast and directs that the findings be brought to the War and Navy Departments.

subfiles.title: Report on the visit of the Japanese naval tanker Ondo
subfiles.from: H. C. Gilchrist, Major, Infantry, commanding Hawaii District
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Hawaiian Department
subfiles.about: Gilchrist reports on the Ondo’s April 1936 visit to Hilo and identifies suspected intelligence collection and local Japanese contacts.
subfiles.summary: The report gives the tanker’s specifications, crew, cargo, itinerary, water intake, and official calls, then records alleged photography, sketching, measurement of Hilo’s docks, unexamined mail and packages, and tours of Waimea and Kona. It profiles Kango Kawasaki, Dr. Yoshimura, Frank Arakawa, Ishikawa, Minoru Murakami, and several others whose conduct was considered suspicious. Gilchrist concludes that Ondo came to collect information, contact agents, and obtain enough water to cruise among Japanese Pacific units before returning to Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding information on Japanese officers near Waimea
subfiles.about: Carter forwards A. A. Akina’s account of Japanese officers visiting Waimea and offers to make further inquiries.
subfiles.summary: Carter links the reported Waimea party to a Japanese oil tanker that left Hilo April 19, regretting that witnesses lacked automobile numbers or driver identities.

subfiles.title: Letter reporting observation of Japanese uniformed men taking bearings near Waimea
subfiles.about: Akina relays Mrs. Kanakanui’s eyewitness account of Japanese uniformed men using an optical instrument and papers to survey the countryside near Waimea.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Kanakanui reportedly saw ten uniformed Japanese and three civilians set up a telescope-like tube and work with large paper sheets near Waimea; Akina notes a Honolulu visitor distributing a Mikado picture.

subfiles.title: Report on Kango Kawasaki’s contacts with Japanese ships
subfiles.to: J. Walter Doyle, Collector of Customs
subfiles.about: Anderson explains why Kango Kawasaki’s repeated assistance to Japanese training ships and tankers appeared suspicious to Hilo customs officials.
subfiles.summary: Anderson says Kango Kawasaki greeted Japanese vessels, accompanied officers with cameras and challenged customs rules; an alien with legal training. Anderson has no concrete evidence of government ties but finds the conduct circumstantially significant.

subfiles.title: Judge Advocate General opinion on Japanese naval and civilian activities in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Judge Advocate General of the Navy
subfiles.about: The opinion evaluates whether reported Japanese reconnaissance, propaganda, and organizational activities in Hawaii could be prosecuted under federal or territorial law.
subfiles.summary: The Judge Advocate General concludes that photographing fortifications, measuring Hilo docks, and taking bearings near Kamuela could fall within the federal Espionage Act if the required intent and evidence were established. The opinion also surveys Hawaiian laws concerning syndicalism, secret associations, unauthorized military organizations, and disloyal propaganda, finding that they supplement federal law. It explains that the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation protects Japanese persons and vessels from discriminatory treatment but does not immunize violations, while potentially limiting blanket exclusion of Japanese shipping; the document continues beyond page 152.
